speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: asked the Minister for Education in light of the recent results of the Survey of Adult Skills under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's (OCED's) Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) which indicate a decline in English literacy skills amongst older workers in Singapore, whether the Ministry has any initiatives in place to help Singaporeans maintain literacy levels as they age.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: asked the Minister for Education in respect of the results of International Assessment of Adult Competencies which is a global test of adult skills conducted by OECD (a) what targeted initiatives are being implemented to address the decline in literacy skills among adults over 35 years old; and (b) how does the Ministry support individuals in multilingual work environments to maintain and enhance their English literacy skills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Education regarding the recent report on the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) (a) whether Singapore’s SkillsFuture programme have objectives that measure outcomes in a similar way to PIAAC in terms of (i) social and economic impact and (ii) performance of education and training system; and (b) whether specific areas of skills to be improved can be drawn from this report to enhance the SkillsFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: My response will also cover the matters raised in the oral Parliamentary Questions (PQs) scheduled for the Sitting on or after 9 January from Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim and the two written PQs scheduled for Sittings on 7 January and on or after 9 January 2025 from Members Ms See Jinli Jean and Dr Wan Rizal, please.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I invite Members to seek clarifications as needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Survey of Adult Skills is developed by the Organisation for Economic and Co-operation Development (OECD) Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) to assess the proficiency of adults in literacy, numeracy and adaptive problem-solving skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are key information processing skills that are used and developed at work and in daily life, and also enable the acquisition of new knowledge and skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Thus far, two PIAAC cycles have been conducted – the first from 2014 to 2015 and the second, more recently, from 2022 to 2023.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Overall, we have made progress since the first PIAAC cycle.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our adaptive problem-solving score was comparable to OECD’s mean.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When comparing adults born in the same years across the two cycles, the OECD also found that nearly half of the countries had substantial age-related skill losses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Further studies will be needed to understand these findings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But these observed trends are likely due to a combination of several factors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In Singapore, our education system has developed rapidly over the past decades and younger cohorts have benefited from significantly improved educational opportunities compared to earlier cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is reflected in the OECD PIAAC scores where our younger adults scored near the top in all three proficiency domains, while older adults scored below the average OECD scores.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what we call the "cohort effect".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the atrophy effect, where acquired skills decline after adults leave the formal education system and enter work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This could be because the skills are not as frequently used or as deliberately honed at work compared to during the formal schooling years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, we also need to be mindful of the obsolescence effect, where skills become less relevant or even obsolete at the workplace, given rapidly changing market demands, technological advancement and enterprise transformation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is also growing research interest on how technology has changed the way we consume and process information, with many people moving away from complex writing to shorter social media posts and videos.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As cognitive outsourcing becomes more prevalent with artificial intelligence (AI), there is also a risk of erosion of deep thinking and reflection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some Members have also asked what the results mean for the competitiveness of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We take part in PIAAC to help gauge our progress in adult continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In that regard, our improvements over the two cycles of testing are encouraging.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, the skills assessed by OECD are not the only skills that affect the employability of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To put together a better picture of where we are, we need to consider other data points as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For instance, whether our workers have job-specific skills is crucial to their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also other metrics that measure the competitiveness of a country or workforce, such as our employment rate, the number of companies that continue to invest good jobs in Singapore and whether our workers command good wages.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Nevertheless, to mitigate the atrophy and obsolescence effects, it is necessary for us to continuously upskill and reskill throughout life, beyond the first 15 years of formal education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Which is why I always emphasise that while we have done well for the first 15 years of our student achievements in school, we must also focus on the next 50 years of our time beyond school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Individuals and employers also have key roles to play.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Individuals must take ownership of their learning journeys throughout life and take steps to constantly upskill and reskill, to push against the natural skills atrophy that the PIACC results suggest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Employers must also stay nimble and transform their business and jobs to compete internationally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They must also invest in their employees’ career health, such as by articulating their company’s skills needs and supporting their employees to undergo training so their employees have the capabilities to successfully achieve employers’ business goals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some have asked how we should interpret the PIAAC results in relation to our overall economic and workforce competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our overall economic and workforce competitiveness also depends on other factors, including but not limited to, our ability to provide a business-friendly environment, consistent policies, stable government and measures to attract complementary talent and skills from the global networks to complement and supplement our own.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These factors contribute to an ecosystem where businesses can make the best use of our workforce’s talent to innovate and thrive.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have just one supplementary question for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider collaborating more with Singapore publishers, booksellers and literary charities to enhance English literacy skills all round?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just to provide some background, we have a number of them in Singapore, for example, Book Bar, Ethos Books, Epigram Books, the Singapore Book Council and SingLit Station, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These entities have very successfully curated and created many interesting talks and lifestyle events that promote a reading culture around Singapore literature or SingLit, for short.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: SingLit stories are not only relatable, but very impactful for a local audience who can see their own life experiences and culture mirrored in the books and stories that they read.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, to reiterate my question, will the Ministry be open to leveraging off of the initiatives of these entities in order to create a better reading culture and accordingly, improve adult literacy skills within the community?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not just encouraging people to read more, but also to read widely and to be more reflective.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we are all conscious of today's media environment, whereby there are so many different channels competing for the attention of our people and we will have to keep up our efforts to continue our encouragement to our people to keep learning, to keep reading even as they are working and have gone beyond the school years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Really, we all have to be aware of this famous dictum: we either use it, hone it, or we lose it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that applies to all the skillsets that we picked up from young and we just have to keep working on it; otherwise, the atrophy effect will set in, regardless of our background.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second one, I would like to also continue on the point that the Minister spoke about skills atrophy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, let me respond to the first on how we help our workers to be more focused and targeted in their selection of training courses and modules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One way that SkillsFuture Singapore does it is that we generally curate a set of courses that we think are industry relevant and we publicise this set of courses to encourage people to take up the courses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why there is a set of curated courses under the SkillsFuture programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, in the care economy, in the green economy and the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond this generic high-level cluster of skills required, we try to drill down to the specifics so that we can have curated programmes for our workers to subscribe to, so that they can improve their skillsets as necessary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What we want to also do is have a broader culture where every one of us – individuals and employers – take ownership of this process to keep upgrading our skillsets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our competition is how we, as a Singaporean workforce, compete with the rest of the world, the best of the world, so that we can continue to find our own niche areas to make a living for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is evergreen work and we must keep doing this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second issue about the age threshold of 40, let me just put in context the SkillsFuture framework of assisting our people to upgrade their skillsets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not a binary thing, where there is a before or after age 40, where we help or do not help people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Actually, we have a suite of schemes that help people from the time they leave school, all the way until they grow much older.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is just that we have intensified our efforts for the post-40, because our surveys, our dipsticks show that that is the most urgent part.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, even for people below the age of 40, we have other SkillsFuture programmes that allow them to access training programmes, as part of the larger SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But in the recent announcement, we have made more and we have intensified our efforts to help those above the age threshold of 40, because that is most critical and most urgent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But given the resources and the urgency of the problem that we have, that is why this year we have made the effort to focus on the post-40 age group.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That does not mean that the pre-40s do not need to upskill.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That does not mean that we have no programmes to help those in the pre-40s.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether we need to step up the efforts, we will continue to review our programmes and make sure that we support Singaporeans accordingly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Minister for the details and what he has shared, in terms of the approach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I just have two supplementary questions because my concern is not so much the exact scores, but the trend of what we are seeing and that the atrophy of skills is in the very basic area of adaptive skills, which is very important if we look at the environment of fast change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is not so much specific skillsets and picking up specific skillsets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From the insights in the report, is there going to be any curation, in terms of how we work with organisations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the age group that is concerning, it is the 35-and-onwards group.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Most of the people will be in the midst of their careers, not so much what age they are, but more in the midst of their careers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are very busy, really just doing their work and so, many times, they neglect their development.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we can talk about all parties being responsible to take up development, they also have to do their work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how do we look at the work itself and working with employers and all stakeholders to say, do we curate it in a way that allows people within the workforce to be able to do their continuous learning?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not easy, but it is something that I think we need to rethink, perhaps the approach of learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not just about going to attend courses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister has rightly said, if you do not use it, even if you learn it, it is not going to be effective.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it is concerning because the trend is worrying – it is adaptive skills, it is the very basic core skills of literacy which affects ability to learn.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope that the Minister can give assurance about the approach that we will take and if there is going to be any refinement in what we do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the first PIACC cycle, they measured two things: numeracy and literacy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the more recent PIACC cycle, they measured three things: numeracy, literacy and problem-solving skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is of concern to us because literacy is the basis upon which we acquire and process information.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For adaptive problem-solving, we have no basis for comparison because the first cycle did not measure this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was the first time that they measured problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But within that, just as we have expected, we see a difference between the younger age group which performed very well, versus the older age group that did not perform so well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But our average for the whole workforce is at the OECD average.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Of course, one can take the argument that with more cohorts coming in, our flow of the cohorts will slowly overturn the stock effect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But to us, that is not satisfactory because that will take us too long for us to want to be competing at the top end of the global league.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, we need to step up our SkillsFuture programme, but the SkillsFuture programme does not address literacy per se.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The SkillsFuture programme addresses the kind of skillsets necessary for that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to couple the SkillsFuture effort, where we target our efforts to improve the skillsets of our people that are job-specific, with a more general culture that Ms Usha Chandradas mentioned; that we need to encourage our people to read, to maintain their literacy proficiency in order to process and manage information, especially in today's bewildering world, where the problem is not a deficit of information; the problem is a deluge of information which becomes bewildering.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we help our people to do the three "Ds", which I always emphasise in MOE?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To "distil" the information; to "discern" with values; and to "discover", meaning to create new value propositions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are the new competencies that we have to encourage our adults to have, starting from school, where we keep emphasising the abilities for our students to distil, discern and to discover.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, what else are we going to do?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to spend much more effort and pay more attention to what we call the adult-learning andragogy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have spent a lot of effort over the previous decades and years on how to build up the science of learning for our school children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More recently, we have also invested in the National Institute of Early Childhood Development (NIEC) to look at the pedagogies and the methods to help our younger cohorts, the preschool cohorts, to build the necessary foundations for their education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we have done this for the school and the preschool, in terms of pedagogical developments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because the same content delivered to a 25-year-old, a 35-year-old, a 45-year-old, will need to be different.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And in fact, the most interesting institution that we have today is the Singapore University of Social Science, because many of their classes have what we call inter-generational students from different backgrounds and it requires different pedagogies or adult andragogy for us to effectively teach and allow and help our adult students to master the content.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like others who read the news, and as an educator myself, I was, of course, alarmed to read about the study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I am a little less convinced than the Minister that the solution necessarily is about doubling down on adult reskilling and upskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Literacy, I believe, is truly a foundational skill, as the Minister and also Ms Jessica Tan mentioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so, reskilling and upskilling necessarily builds on this foundation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder, therefore, in the interest of retaining knowledge and learning, whether there should be programmes right at the earlier levels of the formal schooling level that will foster interest in knowledge and learning acquisition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, that is the first part of my supplementary question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second is, I wonder whether some of this has to do with a mindset that is common in our educational culture to study for the test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Often, we hear about how after the test, we "return" things to the teacher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the high stakes testing culture that we have fostered here may be responsible for this and I wonder if the Minister can share a bit about his thoughts on that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we certainly agree, it is not an either/or thing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The test is but a means for us to let the individual know where you are strong or weak at, so that on that basis, you can be put in a learning environment that best suits you, to help you to continue to grow.
